Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates text generation by leveraging the fact that large language models are often highly confident about the next few tokens. Instead of generating text one token at a time, which is slow because each step requires a full forward pass through the model, speculative decoding uses a smaller, faster "draft" model to predict a sequence of tokens. The main, larger model then evaluates this entire sequence in a single pass.

If the main model agrees with the draft model’s predictions, the entire sequence is accepted, and the process moves to the next chunk. This is a massive speedup because the expensive large model only performs one computation for multiple tokens. If the main model disagrees at any point, it rejects the draft from that point onward and generates the correct token itself, after which the process restarts.

The key to your question is why this doesn’t change the output. The main model is the source of truth. It is never asked to "guess" or "hallucinate" new content; it is only asked to verify or correct the draft. Because the main model’s output is deterministic (or sampled from its own probability distribution) based on the context, and it is the final arbiter of every token, the final text is identical to what the main model would have produced if it had generated every token sequentially. The draft model is merely a proposal engine; it has no authority over the final text.

This method is safe because the verification step is exact. The main model checks the draft against its own internal probabilities. If the draft is wrong, the main model corrects it. If the draft is right, the main model accepts it. There is no approximation or lossy compression involved in the final output. The speedup comes from parallelizing the verification of multiple tokens, not from changing the model’s logic.

For a new engineer, think of it like a proofreader. The draft model writes a paragraph quickly. The main model reads the whole paragraph at once. If it’s perfect, it signs off. If there’s a typo, it fixes just that part and continues. The final document is exactly what the main model would have written, but it got there much faster because it didn’t have to write every word from scratch.

The bottleneck of sequential generation is what you're attacking.

- The small model must be "aligned" — it should produce outputs that the big model would likely produce, or you waste most of the passes.

plain.content:
When you store a key-value pair in a hash map, the map first takes your key and runs it through a hash function, which produces an integer. That integer gets mapped down to an index into a fixed-size array — that's the "bucket" for your pair. The trouble is, two completely unrelated keys can occasionally hash to the same index. This is a collision, and it's not really a bug; it's just arithmetic with a finite number of slots. A good hash function makes collisions rare, but it can't make them impossible.

There are two classic strategies for dealing with collisions. The first is called chaining. Think of each bucket in the array not as a single slot but as the head of a short linked list. When a collision happens, the new pair is simply appended to the list living in that bucket. Lookups work the same way: compute the index, walk the small list, and find your key. In practice most languages use some variant of this, sometimes with an array of elements per bucket that gets promoted to a full list only when it grows. The second strategy is open addressing. Here the array is strictly one element per slot. When you hit an occupied slot, you don't chain; instead you probe — you apply a small deterministic formula to get a *next* candidate index, and keep trying the next candidate until you find an empty slot or a slot with your key. Common probing schemes include linear probing (just keep walking forward: index, index+1, index+2…) or quadratic or double-hashing variants that spread the probes more irregularly. Open addressing tends to have better cache performance because everything lives in one contiguous block, but it does need a bit more careful design to handle deletions, since a "hole" left behind can break the probing sequence for other entries that passed through that spot.

Now, collisions are manageable, but there's a second, subtler problem: the map can fill up. If you have ten million keys crammed into ten-thousand buckets, chaining means each list is on average a thousand entries long, and open addressing means you're probing a very long sequence of occupied slots before finding an empty one. Either way, what used to be an average-case O(1) operation is degrading toward O(n). So hash maps monitor a number called the load factor, which is just the ratio of stored entries to bucket slots. A typical implementation sets a threshold — 0.75 is a very common choice, though some use 0.5 or even 1.0 depending on the tradeoff they want — and the moment that threshold is crossed, the map resizes. Resizing means allocating a brand-new, larger array (most implementations double the old capacity, which keeps the load factor roughly half of what it was), then taking every single key-value pair currently stored and re-hashing it against the new, larger table, scattering it into its new bucket. All the work of reinsertion happens at once, so the resize itself is O(n) rather than O(1), but because it's spread across the amortized cost of many subsequent insertions, the average cost per operation stays constant. You also typically re-check the load factor on deletions (some implementations only shrink when the table gets dangerously *empty*, so they won't shrink after every removal). The net effect is that the map stays perpetually in a regime where collisions are infrequent and probes are short, which is what keeps the whole thing fast on average.

Think of normal autoregressive generation as a single worker at a desk, writing one word at a time. Each word depends on the last, so the worker must finish word *n* before starting word *n+1*. If you are generating a long paragraph, those sequential steps are where the cost lives.

Speculative decoding introduces a second worker: a small, fast model that sits beside the big one. The small model guesses a short stretch—say, four to eight words—at once. Because it is tiny, it spits those guesses out in a fraction of the time the big model would need for just one of those words.

Now the big model steps in and grades the draft. Here is the key move: the big model can evaluate all four or eight guessed words in a single forward pass, rather than sequentially. It reads the context and the proposed words together and decides, for each position, "would I have written this word, or something else?" If every guessed word passes, you have just advanced four or eight positions with one pass through the large network. If the third word is wrong, you keep the first two, discard the rest, and the big model writes its own third word, after which you run the little model again to guess the next few.

The trick that keeps the output identical to what you would get by running only the large model is that the large model is never skipped and never asked to be a good-natured yes-saying rubber stamp. Every single token that lands in your final output has been either accepted by the large model's own probability distribution (it genuinely would have generated that token) or written directly by the large model after a rejection. The small model only serves as a hypothesis generator; it never has veto power. In the rare case the little model keeps guessing wrong and you never get more than one token accepted per pass, you have simply fallen back to normal autoregressive speed, with a small constant overhead—the output is byte-for-byte the same as if the big model had written everything alone.

So you are not approximating, sampling differently, or distilling a shortcut into the weights. You are doing the same decisions, just reordering some of them so that several can be checked at once instead of one at a time. The work that was originally unavoidable—the large model looking at its own distribution—is unchanged; the only thing that changes is that the large model no longer has to wait between each individual token to see whether it agrees with a cheap preliminary guess.

plain.content:
A hash map stores key-value pairs by taking a key, running it through a hash function that produces a number, and then using that number (usually by taking its remainder when divided by the table size) to pick a specific slot in an underlying array. The problem is that two different keys can produce the same number, so they both get sent to the same slot — that's a collision. There are two classic ways a hash map deals with this. One approach, called chaining, is to think of each slot not as holding a single entry but as the head of a little linked list of entries. When a collision happens, the new entry is simply added to the list at that slot. Looking up a key means hashing to the slot, then scanning down the chain until you find the matching key. The other approach, called open addressing, keeps the table as a flat array and, when a collision is found, follows some probing sequence — step to the next slot, or the next slot after that, or a hash-derived offset — until an empty slot is found, and you insert there. The lookup then just walks the same probing path until it hits a matching key or an empty slot. Both strategies work fine in practice, and the exact scheme chosen often depends on the language or library implementing the map, but the underlying tension is the same: collisions are expected to be rare enough that you don't need a whole second lookup mechanism, yet the structure must still *work* correctly whenever they do happen.

Resizing is the mechanism that keeps that "rare enough" assumption true as the map grows. Each entry in the map takes up a slot, and the table has a fixed capacity — say it's an array of 8, then 16, then 32 slots. The hash map tracks a load factor, which is essentially the ratio of the number of entries to the number of slots. As you insert more and more items, that ratio climbs. When it crosses a threshold the implementation has chosen — commonly somewhere around 0.6 to 0.75, though it varies — the table starts doing a lot more collisions, chains get longer, probe sequences get longer, and your average operation time degrades from the ideal O(1) toward something worse. At that moment the map triggers a resize. The implementation allocates a new, larger array — most commonly double the previous capacity — and then it takes every single entry out of the old table, recomputes its hash, and reinserts it into the new, larger array. After the old table is gone, most entries land in distinct slots because the larger table gives the hash values more room to spread out, so the load factor drops back down to a comfortable level and performance recovers. This is why a hash map's "average" time complexity is usually stated as O(1) with an asterisk: a single resize is an O(n) operation, but because you only have to do it logarithmically many times over the course of n insertions, the *amortized* cost of each individual insert stays constant. The practical side effect is that a resize can be briefly disruptive — during it, the old table and the new one coexist, and any in-progress operation may need to be re-routed, so implementations sometimes handle this carefully to avoid blocking readers, or they just accept the tiny hitch since the operation is quick and rare.
